captions.instagram:
How does the immune system work?

Every day your marrow makes about 100 billion new defenders. Push a dirty splinter into the skin and watch neutrophils eat the bacteria, find the one B cell whose receptor fits a virus, and slide a crowd past measles' 93% herd-immunity line.

→ Your immune system is an army of cells spread through a hidden network of vessels and organs.
→ Immune cells are born in the bone marrow, trained in the thymus, and gather in about 600 lymph nodes.
→ When a splinter breaks the skin, vessels widen and leak: that red, warm swelling is inflammation.
→ Neutrophils squeeze out of the blood and swallow the bacteria whole.
→ A dendritic cell catches the virus and shows its pieces to a helper T cell in a lymph node.

youtubeLong.title: How does the immune system work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Every day your marrow makes about 100 billion new defenders. Push a dirty splinter into the skin and watch neutrophils eat the bacteria, find the one B cell whose receptor fits a virus, and slide a crowd past measles' 93% herd-immunity line.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/immuneclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/immuneclear

In this video:
• An army spread through your body. Immune cells are born in the red bone marrow, T cells are trained in the thymus, and they gather in about 600 lymph nodes, the tonsils, the spleen and the gut's Peyer's patches.
• Walls, fire and hungry cells. Skin, the airway's mucus escalator and stomach acid stop most germs.
• Learning the enemy. A dendritic cell carries pieces of a virus to a lymph node and shows them to helper T cells.
• Memory, and training without the danger. Memory cells answer a second attack in a day or two, with 10–100 times more antibody.
• The body's drain and filter. Blood pressure pushes fluid out of capillaries; what isn't drawn back, 2–4 litres a day, drains into dead-end lymph capillaries, is pumped by moving muscles past valves, filtered in lymph nodes and returned to a neck vein.
• When defences misfire. Allergies are overreactions, autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes attack the body itself, and HIV attacks helper T cells but can be controlled with free treatment.
